★ 104: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Maitreya’s Questions on the Ten Grounds. (Chapter 17) (Continued) At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the ‘ten grounds’? How many kinds of bodhisattvas are there? The Buddha told Maitreya: “There are ten kinds of bodhisattvas. What are these ten? First, those who have newly entered the path; second, those who have practiced for a long time; third, those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression; fourth, those who dwell in the stage of birth; fifth, those who dwell in the stage of the final existence; sixth, those who dwell in the stage of the last birth; seventh, those who dwell in the stage of the single-interval; eighth, those who dwell in the stage of the one-returner; ninth, those who dwell in the stage of the non-returner; and tenth, those who dwell in the stage of the stream-enterer. These are called the ten kinds of bodhisattvas. Maitreya asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is meant by ‘newly entered,’ ‘long-time practitioner,’ ‘non-retrogression,’ ‘stage of birth,’ ‘final existence,’ ‘last birth,’ ‘single-interval,’ ‘one-returner,’ ‘non-returner,’ and ‘stream-enterer’? The Buddha told Maitreya: “If a bodhisattva has not yet perfected the roots of goodness and has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, this is called ‘newly entered. If a bodhisattva has already perfected the roots of goodness but has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, this is called ‘long-time practitioner. If a bodhisattva has already attained the stage of non-retrogression, this is called ‘non-retrogression. If a bodhisattva has already attained the stage of non-retrogression and is about to enter the womb of a Tathāgata, this is called ‘stage of birth. If a bodhisattva has already entered the womb of a Tathāgata, this is called ‘final existence. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata, this is called ‘last birth. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the single-interval, this is called ‘single-interval. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the one-returner, this is called ‘one-returner. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the non-returner, this is called ‘non-returner. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the stream-enterer, this is called ‘stream-enterer. Maitreya asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘dwelling in the stage of the single-interval’? What is the meaning of ‘dwelling in the stage of the one-returner’? What is the meaning of ‘dwelling in the stage of the non-returner’? What is the meaning of ‘dwelling in the stage of the stream-enterer’? The Buddha told Maitreya: “If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the single-interval, they will, in their final life, attain the stage of Buddhahood. This is called ‘dwelling in the stage of the single-interval. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the one-returner, they will, in their final life, attain the stage of Buddhahood. This is called ‘dwelling in the stage of the one-returner. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the non-returner, they will, in their final life, attain the stage of Buddhahood. This is called ‘dwelling in the stage of the non-returner. If a bodhisattva has already emerged from the womb of a Tathāgata and dwells in the stage of the stream-enterer, they will, in their final life, attain the stage of Buddhahood. This is called ‘dwelling in the stage of the stream-enterer. Maitreya asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘Buddha-ground’? How many kinds of Buddha-grounds are there? The Buddha told Maitreya: “There are two kinds of Buddha-grounds. What are these two? First, the ground of the Dharma-nature; second, the ground of the transformation body. These are called the two kinds of Buddha-grounds. Maitreya asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the ‘ground of the Dharma-nature’? What is the meaning of the ‘ground of the transformation body’? The Buddha told Maitreya: “The ground of the Dharma-nature refers to the true nature of all phenomena, which is neither born nor extinguished, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, and neither arising nor ceasing. This is called the ‘ground of the Dharma-nature. The ground of the transformation body refers to the various manifestations of the Buddha’s physical form, such as the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, which appear in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings to lead them toward liberation. This is called the ‘ground of the transformation body. Maitreya asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘Dharma-nature’? How many kinds of Dharma-natures are there? The Buddha told Maitreya: “There are three kinds of Dharma-natures. What are these three? First, the Dharma-nature of emptiness; second, the Dharma-nature of signlessness; and third, the Dharma-nature of wishlessness. These are called the three kinds of Dharma-natures. 118 120–140 [The following is a translation of the specified section: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the imagined nature? It is the grasping of names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) based on the objects of the five sense-bases (*pañcaviṣaya*). This is called the imagined nature. Next, Mahāmati, what is the dependent nature? It is the manifestation of the mind (*cittadṛśya*) appearing as various forms due to the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination (*vikalpa*). This is called the dependent nature. Next, Mahāmati, what is the perfected nature? It is the state of the non-existence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature. This is called the perfected nature. Next, Mahāmati, what is the nature of the ultimate truth? It is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), transcends the duality of existence and non-existence, and is not an object of discursive thought (*prapañca*). This is called the nature of the ultimate truth. Mahāmati, these are the four kinds of self-nature. You and other Bodhisattvas should thoroughly understand them. If they are not understood, one will fall into the error of asserting that all things are non-existent (*sarvābhāvavāda*). Therefore, you must cultivate the wisdom that realizes the non-duality of existence and non-existence. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of liberation (*vimokṣa*). What are these three? They are: the liberation of the body (*kāyavimokṣa*), the liberation of the mind (*cittavimokṣa*), and the liberation of wisdom (*jñānavimokṣa*). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the liberation of the body? It is the attainment of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) by means of the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*) and the mastery over the elements (*dhātuvaiśāradya*). This is called the liberation of the body. Next, Mahāmati, what is the liberation of the mind? It is the cessation of the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*cittamanovijñāna*) through the realization that the external world is but the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). This is called the liberation of the mind. Next, Mahāmati, what is the liberation of wisdom? It is the direct realization of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpādadharmakṣānti*) and the entry into the realm of the Tathāgatas. This is called the liberation of wisdom. Mahāmati, these are the three kinds of liberation. You and other Bodhisattvas should cultivate them. By cultivating these liberations, one quickly attains the stage of a Tathāgata and benefits all sentient beings. Thus, Mahāmati, you should abandon all views of self-nature and the views of existence and non-existence, and dwell in the state of non-discrimination and non-manifestation. This is the teaching of the Tathāgatas. 231. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving as a real entity; he does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a real entity.

He does not perceive form as a real entity; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a real entity. He does not perceive the eye as a real entity; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a real entity. He does not perceive forms as real entities; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real entities. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a real entity; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real entities. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a real entity; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a real entity; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the element of earth as a real entity; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real entities. He does not perceive the field of the eye as a real entity; he does not perceive the fields of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the realm of desire as a real entity; he does not perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real entities. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real entities; he does not perceive unconditioned phenomena as real entities. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as a real entity; he does not perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real entities. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as a real entity; he does not perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as a real entity. Why is this? Subhūti, because all these things are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they are not to be cultivated. Because they are not to be cultivated, there is no attainment and no realization. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.”

The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom trains in the six perfections by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, it is because he trains in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a ‘bodhisattva.’”

INTRODUCTION The present work is an attempt to provide a systematic exposition of the Buddhist theory of knowledge (*pramāṇa-vāda*) as it was developed within the Madhyamaka school. While the Madhyamaka tradition is often characterized by its emphasis on the refutation of all conceptual extremes (*prapañca*), it nonetheless possesses a sophisticated epistemological framework that serves as the foundation for its philosophical critique. This introduction aims to situate the Madhyamaka theory of knowledge within the broader context of Indian philosophy, tracing its evolution from the early Abhidharma period through the works of the foundational masters Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva, and culminating in the systematic syntheses of Candrakīrti and Śāntarakṣita. It will demonstrate how the Madhyamikas, while maintaining the ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena, nevertheless employ conventional means of valid cognition (*saṃvṛti-pramāṇa*) to lead sentient beings toward the realization of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The discussion will proceed by first examining the general principles of epistemology accepted by the various schools of Indian thought, with particular attention to the definitions of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and the categories of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Subsequently, the specific contributions of the Madhyamaka school to these categories will be analyzed, focusing on the distinction between the two truths and the role of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) in the attainment of liberation. Through this analysis, it is hoped to clarify the logical coherence and soteriological purpose of the Madhyamaka epistemology. [page 109] I. THE BACKGROUND OF INDIAN EPISTEMOLOGY A. The Definition of Valid Cognition (*Pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) In the Indian philosophical tradition, the term *pramāṇa* refers to the instruments or criteria by which correct knowledge is attained. The primary function of a *pramāṇa* is to produce a cognition that is both new (*anadhigata*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). This definition, though subject to varying interpretations among the different schools, establishes the fundamental requirement that a valid cognition must not merely reflect what is already known, nor should it be a distorted representation of reality. B. Direct Perception (*Pratyakṣa*) and Inference (*Anumāna*) Indian epistemologists generally recognize two principal types of valid cognition: direct perception and inference. Direct perception is defined as a cognition that arises from the contact of the senses with their objects and is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā-apoḍha*). Inference, on the other hand, is a process of reasoning based on the observation of logical marks (*liṅga*) that allow one to infer the existence of a hidden object (*liṅgin*). These two means of knowledge are considered sufficient for the establishment of worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) and the pursuit of spiritual goals. II. THE MADHYAMAKA THEORY OF KNOWLEDGE A. The Two Truths and Epistemology The cornerstone of Madhyamaka philosophy is the doctrine of the two truths: the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). For the Madhyamikas, the conventional truth consists of the world of appearances as experienced by ordinary beings, while the ultimate truth is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of those very appearances. Crucially, the Madhyamaka system maintains that the conventional truth is not a mere illusion but possesses a functional validity within the realm of relative experience. Thus, the means of valid cognition operate primarily within the domain of the conventional, providing the necessary tools for analytical investigation and the eventual transition to the realization of the ultimate. B. Candrakīrti’s Synthesis Candrakīrti (c. 600–650 CE), in his seminal work the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, provides a comprehensive synthesis of the Madhyamaka epistemological position. He argues that while the ultimate truth transcends all linguistic and conceptual categories, the conventional truth must be understood through the lens of the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-catuṣṭaya*). These include direct perception, inference, authoritative testimony (*āgama*), and analogy (*upamāna*). By accepting these means of knowledge, the Madhyamikas are able to engage in dialectical debate and refute the erroneous views of opponents without contradicting the conventional consensus. C. Śāntarakṣita and the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka Synthesis The later Madhyamaka tradition, particularly as represented by Śāntarakṣita (c. 725–788 CE) and his disciple Kamalaśīla, further refined the epistemological framework by integrating elements of the Yogācāra school. In works such as the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and its commentary, they argue that while external objects lack inherent existence, the cognitions that apprehend them do possess a degree of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). This synthesis allows for a more nuanced account of the cognitive process, wherein the conventional validity of cognition is preserved even as its ultimate status is deconstructed. In conclusion, the Madhyamaka theory of knowledge demonstrates a remarkable balance between critical negation and constructive affirmation. By utilizing the conventional means of valid cognition, the Madhyamikas are able to dismantle the reifying tendencies of ordinary thought while simultaneously guiding practitioners toward the liberating insight of emptiness. This epistemological rigor ensures that the Madhyamaka path remains both intellectually coherent and soteriologically effective.

96. Kṛtyakalpataru 1.160–162: On the Duties of Women (Strīdharma) and the Duties of a Wife (Patnīdharma). The duties of women have been described; now the duties of a wife shall be explained. A wife who is devoted to her husband and intent upon his service attains the same world as her husband. By serving her husband with devotion, she obtains heaven even if she is devoid of other virtues. She should always remain under her father’s protection in childhood, under her husband’s protection in youth, and under her son’s protection in old age; she should never be independent. She should not frequent the houses of strangers, nor should she stay at the door or in the marketplace. She should always remain chaste, self-controlled, and diligent in household tasks. She should be skilled in cooking, frugal, and attentive to the needs of her kin. She should be pure in body and speech, and should always perform auspicious rites. She should avoid harshness, anger, and excessive talk, and should be gentle and pleasant in speech. She should not look at the sun, nor should she step over a rope used for milking. She should not wash her feet in a vessel made of bell-metal, nor should she eat from a broken dish. She should not laugh loudly, nor should she show her teeth. She should not run while it rains, nor should she look at her own reflection in water. She should not step on ashes, charcoal, husks, or potsherds. She should not wear garments that are frayed, dirty, or torn. She should not wear garlands or ornaments that are faded or worn out. She should not sleep on a high bed, nor should she sit on a seat without her husband. She should not eat before her husband has eaten, nor should she drink before he has drunk. She should not look at him while he is eating, nor should she converse with him while he is angry. She should not reveal his secrets, nor should she speak ill of him. She should always be cheerful, well-dressed, and adorned with ornaments. She should be intent on the welfare of her husband and should never act against his interests. She should serve the gods, the ancestors, and the guests, and should be devoted to the performance of religious rites. She should be constant in her devotion to her husband, for by such devotion she attains the highest state. Thus have the duties of a wife been declared; by following them, she attains eternal bliss.

43 APPENDIX B
1. Introduction and Declaration in the *Dānasāgara* composed by Ballāladēva. *Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa!*
Those who are the direct recipients of the nectar upon the earth, into whose hands the virtuous place the provisions for the journey to the hereafter—
the meritorious words of the three Vedas emerging from their mouths purify the world.
Salutation to those twice-born ones, whose heads I bow with the agitation of intense devotion. || 1 ||
Indra— the sole kinsman of the universe, the preceptor of the injunctions of the Vedas,

the mountain-range of the lineage for the boundaries of conduct and the practice of the warrior code, the ultimate limit of the foundation of good conduct for those terrified by the Kali age— he whose continuous stream of progeny was severed by the excellence of human virtues, as brilliant as pure gems of noble character.
O descendant of Sena, you have emerged from the earth as its ornament, possessing the beauty of a pearl necklace released by the rains.

There, the moving wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) that adorns the path of the virtuous, delightful with its steady and dense shade, easily accessible for the enjoyment of spontaneous affection by the good,
[stands as] a natural adversary to the multitude of lotus-lakes of the winter season.
Renowned for his own virtues and possessing a sublime majesty, Hemantasena was born. || 3 ||
Thereafter, Vijayasena appeared,
a lord of mountains whose heroic banner was honored throughout the four quarters of the world;
his peaks bore his commands like the Vaijayantī banner.
They are embraced by prostration; they are noble royal lineages. || 4 ||
Fulfilling all hopes, his majesty increased; with showers of wealth, he sprinkled the earth— his field of stainless fame—
and was the supreme among kings, like an untimely rain-cloud for those scorched by wretchedness.
From him was born King Śrī Vallāla, a lord whose very essence was the manifestation of virtues. || 5 ||

The venerable Sārasvata-Tryambaka, a praiseworthy personage on the surface of the earth who compiled the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* and other works, whose eyes were the radiant play of an intellect unencumbered by [worldly] treatises;
[Appendix] He was one who practiced the six rites, an abode of noble conduct, and was renowned for his vow of truth.
Just as Gīṣpati is to Vṛtrāri, so is Aniruddha the preceptor of this lord of men.

Having mastered the essence of all the Purāṇas and Smṛtis through faith in this teacher, and desiring to compose a compendium on gifts (dānanibandha) that brings an end to the defilements of the Kali age; || 7 ||
Stilled by doubts arising from his difficult resolution regarding the determination of the Dharma, which is so hard to comprehend,
this king began the service of the lotus-feet of the Brahmins.

By the instruction of his guru, the illustrious King Vallāla— who possesses a heart made pure by the unfailing grace of boons granted through the combined efforts of the gods on earth (the brahmins), who were constantly satisfied by his service, and from whom all doubts have fallen away— composes this work.
This ocean of gifts, extending to the limits of one's own wisdom, is for the welfare of those possessed of faith.
Having bowed again and again with heads touching the circle of the earth, the lords of the twice-born, who are worthy of worship,
are entreated by the illustrious Uvallahasena with palms joined in steady humility:
"At every opportunity, you must protect this [work] of mine, even for the sake of a small portion of merit performed."
This composition is a common great bridge for those possessing merit to cross the ocean of existence. 10.
The Brāhma, Vārāha, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, and Mātsya;
the Vāmana, Vāyavīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Vaiṣṇava. || 11 ||
The Śaiva, Skānda, Pādma, and Kaurma Purāṇas,
as well as the Purāṇas such as the Kūrma and other ancient scriptures.
The Upapurāṇas have been declared, as well as those that clearly prescribe the rules for giving;
[these include] the first Purāṇa, the Śāmba, and both the Kālikās.
The Nāndī, the one known as Āditya, likewise the Nārasiṃha, that which was composed by Mārkaṇḍeya, and the one called Viṣṇudharmottara; || 14 ||
And he [studied] the scripture known as the Viṣṇudharma, the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa Śruti, the narrative of the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa, and the Mahābhārata Saṃhitā. || 15 ||
Manu, Vasiṣṭha, Saṃvarta, Yājñavalkya, Gautama, Kātyāyana, Jābāli, Vyāsa, and Dānabṛhaspati— || 16 ||
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha, Hārīta, Pulastya, and Viṣṇu;
Śātātapa, Yama, Yogiyājñavalkya, and Devala. || 17 ||
Baudhāyana, Vāṅgirasa, Dānavyāsa, and Bṛhaspati.
The two, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Āpastaṃba, and likewise Śāṭyāyana; || 18 ||
The Gadyavyāsa, the Laghuvyāsa, the Laghuhārīta, the Chandogapariśiṣṭa, and the works of Kātyāyana in their entirety.
Having reflected thus, the Purāṇas, Upapurāṇas, Śrutis,
and Saṃhitās have been compiled for the successful completion of this treatise.
The great gifts (mahādānas) are proclaimed there; first, sixteen are described in sequence, and immediately after that, the ten gifts of mountains.
Then, forty gifts beginning with molasses and ending with cows, each decreasing by one, are to be bound [to the ritual] here in due order according to the rule. (22)
Then there are fifty gifts of forty adorned cows,
followed by three kinds of gifts consisting of herds of adorned cows.
Then there are fifteen gifts of unadorned cows,

— — — — — — *The Sūtra on the Great Vehicle’s Profound Meaning* (Mahāyāna-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra) — — — *Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang* — — — Volume One — — — Chapter One: The Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva — — — At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, at Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, free from afflictions, having attained mastery over their minds, well liberated through wisdom, well liberated in mind, with taintless and stainless vision, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were liberated through perfect knowledge, like great nāgas with dragon-kings as their leaders. There were also many great śrāvakas such as Śāriputra, Mahamaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Nanda, Aniruddha, Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula, and others. There were also many great bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, such as Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and others. At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne made of various jewels, surrounded by these great disciples and great bodhisattvas, expounding the Dharma for them. At that moment, the venerable Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, there are bodhisattvas who, having heard this profound sūtra, do not give rise to fear, doubt, or hesitation, but instead develop a mind of joyful faith and understanding. World-Honored One, how long have these bodhisattvas practiced the bodhisattva path? How deep is their cultivation of roots of goodness? To what extent have they been transformed by the Buddhas? And how much of the Tathāgata’s profound meaning have they realized? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, those bodhisattvas have practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; they have cultivated roots of goodness under immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; they have been transformed by immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; and they have realized the Tathāgata’s profound meaning to a degree that is difficult to fathom. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if these bodhisattvas have already practiced the bodhisattva path for such a long time, why do they still appear to be newly practicing the bodhisattva path? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, it is because these bodhisattvas have attained the power of skillful means and the power of wisdom that they manifest as newly practicing the bodhisattva path. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the power of skillful means, and what is the power of wisdom? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, the power of skillful means refers to the bodhisattva’s ability to enter the various realms of existence according to the inclinations of sentient beings, yet without being defiled by the afflictions of those realms. The power of wisdom refers to the bodhisattva’s realization of the emptiness of all phenomena, yet not abandoning the practice of the bodhisattva path. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘profound’? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, ‘profound’ means that which is difficult to understand, difficult to realize, and difficult to enter. It is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which cannot be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘difficult to understand’? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, ‘difficult to understand’ means that the nature of all phenomena is beyond conceptualization and beyond verbal expression, yet it can be realized through the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘difficult to realize’? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, ‘difficult to realize’ means that the ultimate truth is non-dual and non-conceptual, yet it can be realized through the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘difficult to enter’? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, ‘difficult to enter’ means that the gate of the Dharma-realm is vast and boundless, yet it can be entered through the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if the nature of all phenomena is beyond conceptualization and verbal expression, how does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, although the nature of all phenomena is beyond conceptualization and verbal expression, the Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means, teaches the Dharma by means of names, phrases, and syllables, in order to lead sentient beings to realize the ultimate truth. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of names, phrases, and syllables, how can sentient beings avoid falling into the view of grasping at signs? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, when sentient beings hear the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, they should contemplate that names, phrases, and syllables are all empty and illusory, and that the true nature of all phenomena is originally free from such designations.

By thus contemplating, they will not fall into the view of grasping at signs. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if the true nature of all phenomena is originally free from designations, why do sentient beings give rise to various views and attachments? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, it is because sentient beings have accumulated false thoughts and habitual tendencies since beginningless time that they give rise to various views and attachments. The Tathāgata, through the power of great compassion, teaches the Dharma to cause them to abandon these false thoughts and realize the true nature of all phenomena. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if sentient beings can abandon false thoughts and realize the true nature of all phenomena, what is the fruit of this realization? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, the fruit of this realization is the attainment of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, the fulfillment of the six perfections, and the liberation of all sentient beings. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if the Tathāgata’s omniscience is the fruit of realizing the true nature of all phenomena, then all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also realize the true nature of all phenomena. Why is it that they do not attain the Tathāgata’s omniscience? The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Maitreya, although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas realize the true nature of all phenomena, they lack the power of great compassion and the vow to liberate all sentient beings. Therefore, they do not attain the Tathāgata’s omniscience. Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if

[Appendix [[pages 496–496]] Bl] The *Bhāṣya* on the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*. Chapter 10: On the Means of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa*). Section 1: On Direct Perception (*pratyakṣa*). Sūtra 1: Direct perception is that which arises from the contact of the self with the mind, the mind with the sense organs, and the sense organs with their objects. (VS 3.1.13) Commentary: Here, "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to the cognition produced by the contact of the self (*ātman*) with the internal organ (*manas*), the internal organ with the sense organs (*indriya*), and the sense organs with their respective objects (*artha*). This is the definition of direct perception. In this context, "contact" (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the causal condition for the arising of the cognition. Since the contact between the self and the mind is the primary cause for the production of all cognitions, it is mentioned first. The mention of the contact between the mind and the sense organs follows because it is the specific cause for the production of sensory cognitions. Finally, the contact between the sense organs and their objects is mentioned as the cause for the apprehension of the specific qualities of those objects. Thus, the sequence of these contacts is established according to their causal efficacy. Regarding the term "self": it is the substratum of consciousness, distinct from the body, the senses, and the mind. "Mind" is the internal organ, which is the instrument of thought and the medium for the self's connection with the external senses. "Sense organs" are the five faculties—olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory—which serve as the instruments for perceiving their respective objects. "Objects" are the six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence. In this system, direct perception is classified as being of two kinds: that which consists of the cognition itself and that which consists of the object of cognition. However, since the sūtra primarily concerns the means of knowledge, it defines direct perception as the cognitive event arising from the aforementioned contacts. This establishes the foundational nature of direct perception as the primary means of valid cognition.

One who is overcome by the aforementioned [faults] and touched by defects is not desired [as a teacher]. The partial transgression of the Veda is [remedied] by the imperishable [recitation] of even a slightly deficient portion. "Nibhṛta" means tranquil. "Laukika" refers to knowledge acquired through wealth and so forth. "Nivṛta" means free from prohibited and desire-driven actions. "Niṣkriya" means devoid of activities such as the acquisition of wealth.

In sacrifices and other such rites, when one is overcome—that is, rendered inferior—among people previously described by defects such as minor offenses (*upapātaka*) regarding learning and conduct; Vasiṣṭha says:
"That which is neither a sacrificial session (*satra*), nor a non-session, neither learned, nor highly learned..."
No one, even if he were a Brāhmaṇa, knows whether another is well-behaved or ill-behaved.

The intended meaning is that he who belongs to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, who has turned away from wickedness, and who does not openly manifest self-exaltation in this world, is a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Yama and Śātātapa [state]:
"Austerity, the dawning of dharma, truth, purity, knowledge, compassion, and mercy..."
Knowledge, discipline, and non-stealing—this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.

Yoga, austerity, compassion, charity, truthfulness, purity, mercy, self-restraint, learning,
realized knowledge, and faith— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
Forgiveness, self-restraint, compassion, charity, righteousness, truthfulness, sacred learning, and pity— these are [the qualities].
Knowledge, discernment, and faith—this is the defining characteristic of a brāhmaṇa.
Some, however, say that knowledge, austerity, truth,
as well as charity, sacred learning, and yoga— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.

One who is devoid of both knowledge and austerity is merely a Brahmin by birth. Among those who are learned and those who are unlearned, some are wise while others are dull-witted; such is the nature of human beings.
In the second verse, Manu and Vasiṣṭha regard Yama as the supreme deity:

"But those who are not learned in the Vedas, who do not maintain the sacred fires, and who follow the dharma of Śūdras, are not worthy of [hearing] the words [of the law]; regarding this, men cite the following verse."
A Brahmin does not become a matricide by [these acts]: he is not a merchant, nor an actor; he should not perform service for a Śūdra, nor be a thief, nor a physician.
The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms without observing vows or studying the Vedas; for it provides sustenance to thieves.
The sage Śātātapa declared that there are six who are called non-Brāhmaṇas. Śātātapa said:
"Of them, the first follows the conduct of a king, and the second is a buyer and seller."
The third is the slayer of combatants; the fourth is the village priest;
and the fifth is the wage-earner for them, whether of a village or a city.

But a twice-born man should not perform the morning worship before sunrise, nor the evening worship after sunset; the meaning is that for one of little learning, [the reward] is small, while for one of great learning,
it is great.

Having prostrated before the primordial God, the Lord of Lakṣmī...

I shall, with diligent effort, perform that which is the most excellent, which is gracious toward its devotees, and which is manifested by Indra and the other gods— a practice whose essence is abundant giving.
But when there is faith, O Lord of the Waters, the essence of which is generosity, the Wheel-turner proceeds in due order for the benefit and joy of the world.
First is the essential nature of giving, followed by its various classifications;
and then their diverse fruits arising from time, place, and other factors.
The factors of giving, its specific qualities, and all other elements beyond them—
such as the recipient, the object, the place, and the time— are now examined by one of auspicious intellect.
Their fruit is also said to arise in various ways;
thereafter follows the measurement of gold, silver, and so forth.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and the altar (vedī) are well-defined;
furthermore, the sixteen great gifts (mahādāna) are clearly described in their proper sequence.
The scales, the golden embryo, the horse, the cosmic egg, the wish-fulfilling tree,
a thousand cows, gold, a milch cow, and two horses follow in succession.
Then there was a chariot made of gold, adorned with golden horses, chariots, cattle, and other such things. (1)
Then follows the gift of five ploughs, and after that, the gift of land.
The universal wheel, the wish-fulfilling creeper, the seven oceans, the jewel-cow, and the great elemental bell— these are the sixteen gifts.
Thereafter, the ten great gifts (mahādāna) are proclaimed;
first is the gift of gold, and after that, the gift of horses.
The gift of sesame seeds, the gift of an elephant, the gift of a female slave, and the gift of a chariot;
the gift of a house, the gift of land, and thereafter the gift of a maiden.
The gift of a Kapila cow, and the ten gifts in their proper sequence;
first the gift of the Ānandanidhi, and after that the Bhadranidhi.
Next, the gift of the crest (śikhādāna) is supreme, granting all desires;
after that, the great gifts (atidānas) are described in sequence, beginning with the first.
The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and thereafter that of Sarasvatī;
all the gifts of embodied forms will be described clearly and in sequence.
The gift of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, the gift of Gopālaka,
the gift of Varāha, and that of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa belong to Hari.

7–12 [[page 569–569]] + The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to take all the grass, wood, branches, and foliage found within this Jambudvīpa and burn them in a fire, and if someone were to pour a single drop of water upon that fire, would that fire be extinguished by that single drop of water?

“Certainly not, Blessed One. “Ānanda, even more so than that fire, the fire of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is far greater. If a person were to generate a single thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), that fire of the afflictions would be extinguished by that single thought of awakening. Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not abandon the thought of awakening until I have attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this exposition of Dharma? How should it be remembered? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this exposition of Dharma is called ‘The Chapter on the Thought of Awakening’; remember it as such. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the Venerable Ānanda and the assembly of monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had taught. 7–12 [[page 569–569]] + The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many qualities must a monk possess to be considered a true renunciant? The Blessed One replied: “Kāśyapa, a monk must possess four qualities to be considered a true renunciant. What are these four? First, he does not abandon the thought of awakening. Second, he does not disparage others. Third, he does not harbor malice toward sentient beings. Fourth, he does not seek out faults in others. Kāśyapa, a monk who possesses these four qualities is considered a true renunciant. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said: “Blessed One, what is the name of this exposition of Dharma? How should it be remembered? The Blessed One said: “Kāśyapa, this exposition of Dharma is called ‘The Chapter on the True Renunciant’; remember it as such. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
